crime.value: Apparent murder: Janos, a Hungarian hammer thrower, hurls the Russian commissar Boris overboard into the fog. Central question: will the killing be discovered — and did Boris actually die?
crime.quote: Boris and his scream fly through a thin patch in the fog and over the ship’s rail.

victim.value: Boris Volakov, Russian team commissar — feared and hated, a greedy opportunist and black marketeer who coerced female athletes with threats of exile, making him a natural target
victim.quote: He is greedy and opportunistic... in Russia he was a speculator in the black market

closed_world.value: A Russian ship carrying athletic teams across the ocean to New York, fog-bound and slowed, with a fixed shipboard population
closed_world.quote: On the upper deck of this Russian boat which travels to the sports meet in the United States

culprit_and_motive.value: Janos, the Hungarian hammer thrower, acting in rage to protect Nadia from Boris's sexual assault (having earlier plotted to lure Boris into defecting via a fake rich-defector story)
culprit_and_motive.quote: I immediately grasp him by one arm and one leg and swing him in a circle. . .once. . .twice. . .and then I let go.

resolution.value: Bela the pole vaulter reveals Boris survived, landing on a passing freighter's lifeboat, declared himself a refugee — but the ship was Russian; Janos is safe and marries Nadia, with Mariska revealed as his sister
resolution.quote: the ship upon which you tossed him turned out to be a Russian freighter.

investigator.value: Janos, the first-person Hungarian hammer thrower — perpetrator and narrator, investigating his own predicament
investigator.quote: For myself, I throw my weight around—which is the hammer.

suspect_architecture.value: Not a whodunit: the culprit (narrator Janos, Hungarian hammer thrower) is known from the start. Peripheral figures — Mariska (jealous rival, later revealed as his sister), Nadia (the pursued Russian sprinter), and Bela the pole vaulter — function less as suspects than as witnesses/accomplices, with Boris Volakov as the universally disliked victim whose many enemies (dismissed women athletes, cowed team members) would provide a wide field of motive.
suspect_architecture.quote: Boris is a most unpopular man. He is commissar for the Russian team, plus in overall charge of the voyage.

red_herring.value: The fabricated cousin Stephen and his agent 'John Smith of State Street, Chicago' — a bait story invented to lure Boris into defecting; also the false rumour that Boris drank too much and fell asleep aboard, and the planted misdirection that Mariska is a jealous romantic rival rather than the narrator's sister.
red_herring.quote: When I rise to leave Boris is still thinking about my cousin Stephen, who does not exist.

clue_fairness.value: Fair-play clues are seeded in scene: the heavy fog and near-collisions with other ships in crowded traffic lanes are shown before Boris's survival on a passing freighter is revealed; Boris's opportunism and greed are stated before he defects for money; Mariska's odd non-reaction and the narrator's 'we have planned upon this for a long time' precede the sister reveal.
clue_fairness.quote: Even so, we almost run into other ships, for we are now near New York and the traffic lanes are heavy.

social_world.value: Cold War Eastern-bloc athletic hierarchy aboard a Soviet ship: the commissar holds sexual and career power over athletes, dissenters are exiled to teaching calisthenics beyond the Arctic Circle; satellite-nation resentments (Hungarians, Czechs vs Slovakians, Ruthenians) and the prestige of team membership bind everyone.
social_world.quote: “He is the commissar of the athletes,” she says bitterly, “but in his life he has yet to run even the one hundred meter dash.”

alibi.value: The pair consider and reject alibi strategies — a sole confession, or claiming to have witnessed an accidental fall — settling instead on simple denial plus a rumour of Boris sleeping off drink; Nadia's being seen leaving the ballroom with him undermines any alibi.
alibi.quote: “But you were seen leaving the ballroom with him,” I say. “There will be questions asked.”

reveal_mechanic.value: Testimony at the wedding: Bela reports that Boris himself, alive, named his assailant — the fling landed him on a lifeboat canvas of a passing freighter, which proved to be Russian, so his accusation and his radiogram to 'John Smith' are neutralised. The narrator's own final line reveals Mariska is his sister.
reveal_mechanic.quote: “Unfortunately for Boris, the ship upon which you tossed him turned out to be a Russian freighter.”

media_and_audience.value: Narrative control is the weapon: the defector memoir industry ('I Was a Commissar for the F.B.I.') as capitalist packaging of Cold War stories, the ship's loudspeaker paging the missing Boris, the drunk-asleep rumour the culprits seed, and the fear that public exposure would make America refuse to shield a murderer.
media_and_audience.quote: There is a rumor—which Nadia and I have started—that Boris has drunk too much and fallen asleep in some corner of the ship.

investigator_wound.value: Janos, the amateur schemer-narrator, is vulnerable through his chivalric temper: his cold plan to lure Boris away collapses when fury overrides calculation, and afterwards his new life and marriage rest on a killing that exposure would destroy.
investigator_wound.quote: fury springs into my blood and I forget all about Mohammedans and their mountains.

victims_enemies.value: Boris Volakov, the Russian team commissar, is universally disliked: he coerces female athletes sexually and exiles those who refuse (three women now teaching calisthenics near the Arctic Circle), his reports cause athletes to 'disappear,' and he has a history in Budapest that offends the Hungarians. His enemies include Nadia (his current target), Janos (her would-be protector), and effectively the whole ship.
victims_enemies.quote: It is a rumor that his unfavorable reports have caused the disappearance of one high jumper, one long distance runner, and one hop, skip, and jump.

suspect_wounds.value: Janos is a hammer thrower — his very athletic gift (throwing weight around) makes him the obvious candidate for hurling a man overboard; and as a planned defector he cannot afford scrutiny. Nadia is vulnerable because she was publicly seen leaving the ballroom with Boris. Mariska's jealousy of Nadia gives her the look of motive too.
suspect_wounds.quote: “But you were seen leaving the ballroom with him,” I say. “There will be questions asked.”

unreliable_frame.value: Janos narrates in first person and is a self-serving liar: he invents an entire fictitious cousin Stephen and his best-selling book to bait Boris, conceals his 'clever plan' from Nadia and the reader, and withholds until the final line that Mariska is his sister, not his lover — a deliberate misdirection of the reader's romantic assumptions.
unreliable_frame.quote: When I rise to leave Boris is still thinking about my cousin Stephen, who does not exist.

setting_as_constraint.value: A closed Soviet ship bound for New York: no escape, commissar surveillance, forced attendance at the Friendship Party. The dense fog near New York — ship slowed to a halt, horns blowing, heavy traffic lanes — both muffles Boris's scream (concealing the crime) and, unseen, places a passing freighter beneath him that saves his life and undoes the deed.
setting_as_constraint.quote: there comes a thick fog upon the ocean and it is necessary for the ship to slow almost to a halt and blow its horns often

evidence_type.value: Testimonial — the survivor's own account. Boris, alive, names Janos as the man who threw him overboard, relayed secondhand by Bela the pole vaulter at the wedding. No physical or forensic proof exists.
evidence_type.quote: “No. But I have just heard that Boris himself maintains that this happened.”

false_suspect.value: No true false suspect; suspicion, if any, would fall on Nadia, the last person seen leaving with Boris, though the act was entirely Janos's. She proposes covering it up and thereby shares exposure without guilt.
false_suspect.quote: “We will say it was an accident which we both witnessed. Boris slipped and fell overboard.”

technical_detail.value: Hammer-throwing technique: Janos grips Boris by one arm and one leg and spins him twice before releasing — a 'world's record' fling. The very specialization established in the first paragraph ('I throw my weight around—which is the hammer') both enables and identifies the culprit.
technical_detail.quote: I immediately grasp him by one arm and one leg and swing him in a circle. . .once. . .twice. . .and then I let go.

moral_ambiguity.value: Janos acts not from calculation but from fury at witnessing an assault — his scheme had been the bloodless one of luring Boris to defect through greed. The 'victim' is a corrupt opportunist and sexual predator, and his ultimate punishment is delivered by his own greed and the Russian freighter, not by the killer.
moral_ambiguity.quote: When I see what could be impending, fury springs into my blood and I forget all about Mohammedans and their mountains.
